newsitem.title: UK: UK budget outlook-shares nervous over tax changes.
newsitem.headline: UK budget outlook-shares nervous over tax changes.

text.p: Britain's stock market has already spent weeks fretting about Wednesday's budget and remains fixated on the possible abolition of tax breaks which boost the value of shares to pension funds, analysts said on Friday.

Yet after a sharp drop earlier this month, the market may have already priced in the worst impact of the removal of the dividend tax credit for pension funds -- the biggest investors in the UK stock market, with shares worth about 600 billion stg.
"All this has been talked about enough", said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon, adding he saw the FTSE 100 at worst down to around 4,500 -- three percent below its current level.

The issue of the dividend tax credit however remains a crucial one for the UK equity market, in a budget which could have a determining impact on the outlook for the British economy and UK shares through the rest of the year.

If Chancellor (finance minister) Gordon Brown delivers a market-friendly package, with just the right mix of tax-raising measures to prevent the economy overheating, the market could spike higher just as it did when he gave interest rate independence to the Bank of England.
Yet a clumsy budget, seen as anti-business, could weight on the market for some time to come.
The market's sensitivity to the tax credit issue has already been clearly signalled.
The FTSE 100 index lost more than five percent from its all-time high of 4,796 points on June 13, after a press report said Brown would abolish the tax credit.
For pension funds the credit is an important measure -- it means they can reclaim the 20 percent Advance Corporation Tax which companies pay on their dividends.
Ironically the previous Conservative government has already tinkered with the system, cutting ACT and thereby reducing the amount reclaimable by pension funds.

A Reuters poll of analysts showed that 60 percent expected ACT would either be reduced to ten percent this time or would be phased out over a five-year period. Only 15 percent expected Brown to scrap ACT entirely.
The issue remains crucial for the valuation of the stock market and not only the pension funds would suffer, analysts say.
Nearly half of the companies in the FTSE 100 index would would find their pension funds underfunded if the tax credit is axed, said brokerage BZW in a recent study.
BZW said companies would have to increase their pension contributions to offset the effect of the loss of dividend income, giving a noticeable blow to their profitability.

Those most affected would be companies which have cut their workforces in recent years but still carry pension liabilities from former employees -- and those which still employ large numbers of staff.
Companies like British Steel, Imperial Chemical Industries, British Telecom and British Airways could face profit drops ranging from five to 20 percent, BZW reckoned.

A squeeze on such firms could effectively run counter to Brown's stated objective of encouraging investment and would also target companies which have already been squeezed by the strength of the pound.
"Many of those worst affected are the companies he would least wish to hit -- manufacturers," said BZW.

"They are already suffering enough thanks to sterling strength. This is another reason to question whether a change in the tax credit should happen at all...We would still look out for an offset perhaps related to the policy mix or to investment that softens the blow..."
Most in the market remain convinced that some change is inevitable.

"Abolishing ACT would earn Brown five million pounds. He might be tempted to do it because it would be easy", said Richard McGuire at Salomon Brothers, adding this risk had not yet been fully reflected in share prices.

Under McGuire's worst scenario, under which ACT is completely axed and the planned "windfall" tax on privatised utilities goes ahead, the FTSE would have to plunge to 3,750 points to offer similar yields as now.
BZW strategist Steve Wright said he expected a "big but reasonable" budget.
"They (the Labour government) are determined to do what they have promised," Wright said. "But they will also be concerned about how the budget is perceived in the market."
